🔴Not every belief that keeps us alive is necessarily true. "Practical usefulness does not imply theoretical truth." ✍ Mostafa Malekian

🔹The fact that a belief helps us in practice, solves a problem, or even contributes to our survival does not by itself show that the belief corresponds to reality. Being useful is one thing; being true is another. You cannot infer the latter from the former.

A medicine may cure our headache, yet the theory on which the medicine was based may not be correct. The drug's effectiveness in curing does not by itself prove the correctness of the theory behind it.

The same distinction must be kept in mind in the discussion of evolution. If we accept Darwin's theory, we must note that the persistence of our beliefs, feelings, emotions, and desires does not necessarily mean they show us the truth; they may have persisted because they helped preserve the survival of our species.

That something ensures the survival of the human species is different from its expressing the truth. We may have held a belief, and that very belief kept our species alive; but from this one cannot conclude that the belief was certainly correct. It is even possible that awareness of a truth, rather than aiding our survival, endangers it.

🔹When people have said since ancient times that "the truth is bitter," one of its meanings is this: what is true is not always life-preserving for us or a guarantor of our continued existence.

🔹Therefore, even if a belief seems perfectly clear and self-evident to us and generation after generation has lived with it, this mere persistence and usefulness does not prove that it is true.

🔹From the fact that "this belief has helped our survival," one cannot conclude that "therefore this belief is true."

➖Part of the lecture "Critique_of_the_Book_Analytical_Idealism" @mostafamalekian

🔴Can one be a materialist without denying God? | The difference between materialism and moral materialism ✍ Mostafa Malekian

Materialism comes in two very distinct forms: one is "philosophical materialism" and the other is "moral materialism" or "value materialism." To clarify the difference, we need to see what each one claims.

Who is a materialist in the philosophical sense?

Philosophical materialism is a view of the universe. Those who hold this view believe that nothing exists in the world unless it is the product of the exchange of matter and energy—that is, the product of matter converting into energy or energy converting into matter.

🔹But what about our mind and our mental states? Materialists hold two positions here: Some say that mind and mental states do not exist at all. If we ask why we believe they exist, they answer that this belief is a product of our "folk psychology"; it is within this psychology that something called mind and mental states appears to exist.

🔹Others say that mind and mental states do exist, but they are reducible to the same exchange of matter and energy. In a sense, mind and mental phenomena too seem to be wearing a disguise; otherwise, they too are simply material phenomena.

🔹With such a view, one can no longer believe in the existence of God or a non-material spirit and soul. This is philosophical materialism—a view that many philosophers have held throughout history.

But what is moral materialism?

Moral materialism has nothing to do with philosophical materialism at all; rather, it is a theory in axiology whose gist is this: the only thing that matters in life is wealth.

Here I use "wealth" in a sense that also includes money, property, and assets.

If you believe that in human life only one thing has value, and that is wealth, you are a moral materialist. Since value means having importance, it can be put more simply: in this view, only wealth is important and nothing else in life matters.

According to this view, wealth—for having a good and ideal life—is both a "necessary condition" and a "sufficient condition":

• Necessary condition means that unless you are wealthy, you will not have a good life.

• Sufficient condition means that if you have wealth, you no longer need anything else for a good life.

Most of us human beings, in most historical periods, have not been materialists in the first sense; but the majority of us are materialists in the second sense.

➖From the lecture "Balance and Equilibrium between Money and Spirituality"

entry.summary:
Machine-translated from the original Telegram post.

Source: @mostafamalekian

🔴I Have Not Been Happy ✍️ From an interview with Mostafa Malekian. Published in Andishe Pouya 102

You have always said that spirituality is a process that brings tranquility, joy, and hope. As you pass seventy, have you yourself attained this tranquility, joy, and hope?

🔹As for tranquility, I am content and I believe I have it. As for hope, I am also content. But joy, no. From childhood onward, I think — perhaps due to my psychological makeup, or perhaps due to my childhood environment — I have fundamentally never been happy. This one thing I truly lack, and I have never truly laughed from the bottom of my heart; never.

Looking back on your life from the vantage point of seventy, what was the hardest period of your life? And what was the most precious price you paid for intellectual honesty?

🔹I think the most precious price I paid was losing friends. I am a person who cherishes friendship, and friendship matters greatly to me. To this day, I myself have never cut ties with anyone. But with every intellectual transformation I underwent, I lost a number of friends for whom I was very dear. It was as though their beliefs mattered more to them, and when I changed my beliefs, they would sever their friendship with me.

🔹The hardest period of my life was when I forsook many outward trappings and privileges in order to bring about, in my own estimation, a transformation in the Qom seminary. At that time I was also devout in every sense; out of compassion and mercy, I wanted the educational, training, and research system of the seminary to change so that the very goals they held would be realized and achieved in the best possible way. For example, I myself began changing the textbooks — that is, I was teaching, but not with the seminary textbooks, rather with books I deemed better. But gradually I saw that I was far too small to accomplish anything against this very old edifice. During those eighteen years in which I wanted to do something in Qom, I was awarded a scholarship twice to be sent abroad, and I went neither time. It always seemed to me that if this transformation took place in the seminaries, it would be more beneficial for society. But I returned unsuccessful. In the year 1372, after much pressure, I came and bought a house in Tehran and returned to Tehran to live. Again some of the gentlemen insisted that no, stay in the seminary. I gave back the very house I had bought in Tehran, and returned to Qom once more, staying there another seven years until the year 1379. But I saw that everything was falling apart.
